reason: Most of the weight sits on bills that give people who served, mostly reservists in the Swords of Iron war, priority or extra benefits. These include tuition aid (1, 2, 17, 20), land priority (3), daycare (7, 9, 34), property-tax discounts (8, 19), income-tax credits (11, 28, 35, 37), national-insurance benefits (15, 21, 24), and priority in tenders and civil-service hiring (6, 26). The status-of-the-serviceman bills (16, 23, 36) are also in this group. A smaller set of main-label bills takes support away from those who did not serve: child allowance (22), funding of institutions (18, 30), aid for Torah learners (29) and housing benefits (40). That is the same quantity, benefits linked to service, seen from the other side. The current statement's 'even if others get less' already covers it, so a split is not needed. Its examples (tuition, daycare, tax breaks, land) match the heaviest bills, and the agree key ('+') matches every label. Two bills tie political rights rather than benefits to service: voting (5) and membership in the cabinet security committee (39). They are a different issue, but they point the same way and carry little weight, so they do not justify a rewrite.
